newsitem.title: SPAIN: Q1 data fires Spanish hopes of 200,000 new jobs.
newsitem.headline: Q1 data fires Spanish hopes of 200,000 new jobs.

text.p: Spain created 402,600 jobs in the last 12 months, 49,400 of those in the 1997 first quarter alone, making an official forecast for an additional 200,000 to 250,000 new posts this year even more likely, analysts said on Monday.
"Simply multiplying the first quarter data by four you get 200,000 more jobs," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"But I would expect the second, and the third quarters to create more jobs (than the first) at least, for seasonal reasons as tourism picks up (towards the summer)," he added.
Spain, which has the highest unemployment rate in Europe, is expecting to end the year with at least 200,000 new jobs, according official government forecasts as of this year.
Earlier on Monday the quarterly job survey by the National Statistics Institute INE, normally seen as the most reliable jobs data, showed a modest but consistent decline in the jobless rate.
The survey showed jobless in the first quarter fell to 21.49 percent from 21.78 percent in the fourth quarter.

That compared favourably with 22.91 percent in the first quarter of the previous year. Although changes made more than one year ago in the way the survey is carried out does not make the figures directly comparable, economists welcomed the fall.
"This really is very good news," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
Spain's other jobs indicator, published monthly by the Labour Ministry, is based on those who register for jobless benefits. The rate stood at 13.6 percent in April.
According to the INE survey new jobs rose 3.3 percent in the first quarter of 1997 versus the year-ago period.
But analysts said new jobs were still not enough to fuel private consumption and economic growth, at least that is until the new jobs become permanent.
"We have had strong employment growth in the last eight quarters at rate of 2.5 percent or higher, said Urrutia.
"But I would not be overly optimistic, at least not while the new jobs created are mostly on a temporary basis".

After the recent approval of a pact to reform Spain's rigid labour market, firms now have the possibility of making temporary jobs permanent with the incentive of sharp discounts in social security payments.
Economists expect this measure to boost permanent job creation.
Given such a high level of unemployment, the rate of activity among women is still very low when set against the European average.
That means that any rise in the number of workers is increasingly concentrated in the female workforce, analysts said.
In the first quarter the rate of unemployment among women was 28.61 percent, while among men it was 17.0 percent.
